claim: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disease which affects 1 in every 3500 boys.
source: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disease which affects 1 in every 3500 boys resulting in progressive muscle atrophy, loss of ambulation and cardio-respiratory failure (Levi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levi et al., 2015.

claim: DMD results in progressive muscle atrophy, loss of ambulation and cardio-respiratory failure.
source: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disease which affects 1 in every 3500 boys resulting in progressive muscle atrophy, loss of ambulation and cardio-respiratory failure (Levi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levi et al., 2015.

claim: In DMD patients, the leading cause of mortality is diaphragm dysfunction.
source: In DMD patients, the leading cause of mortality is diaphragm dysfunction (Finder et al., 2004; Finsterer and Stöllberger, 2003; Percival et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finder et al., 2004; Finsterer and Stöllberger, 2003; Percival et al., 2012.

claim: In the mdx animal, disease progression in the diaphragm mimics the human development of the disease.
source: In the mdx animal, a mouse model of DMD, disease progression in the diaphragm mimics the human development of the disease (Stedman et al., 1991), and respiratory dysfunction has been shown to promote cardiac dysfunction (Barbin et al., 2016; Finder et al., 2004; Lanza et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stedman et al., 1991.

claim: Respiratory dysfunction has been shown to promote cardiac dysfunction in mdx mice.
source: In the mdx animal, a mouse model of DMD, disease progression in the diaphragm mimics the human development of the disease (Stedman et al., 1991), and respiratory dysfunction has been shown to promote cardiac dysfunction (Barbin et al., 2016; Finder et al., 2004; Lanza et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barbin et al., 2016; Finder et al., 2004; Lanza et al., 2001.

claim: Nox2 content and activity are upregulated prior to the onset of inflammation and necrosis in dystrophic muscle.
source: Nox2 content and activity are upregulated prior to the onset of inflammation and necrosis (Whitehead et al., 2010) and downregulating Nox2 ROS production protects against pathophysiological alterations in young (5–7 wk) dystrophic muscle (Pal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whitehead et al., 2010.

claim: Downregulating Nox2 ROS production protects against pathophysiological alterations in young (5–7 wk) dystrophic muscle.
source: Nox2 content and activity are upregulated prior to the onset of inflammation and necrosis (Whitehead et al., 2010) and downregulating Nox2 ROS production protects against pathophysiological alterations in young (5–7 wk) dystrophic muscle (Pal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pal et al., 2014.

claim: The microtubule (MT) network is dysregulated in dystrophic muscle.
source: Recent evidence indicates the microtubule (MT) network is dysregulated in dystrophic muscle (Belanto et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2017; Khairallah et al., 2012; Prins et al., 2009), which results in aberrant Nox2 ROS production and implicates Nox2 ROS in altered mechanotransduction (Khairallah et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Belanto et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2017; Khairallah et al., 2012; Prins et al., 2009.

claim: Dysregulation of the MT network results in aberrant Nox2 ROS production.
source: Recent evidence indicates the microtubule (MT) network is dysregulated in dystrophic muscle (Belanto et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2017; Khairallah et al., 2012; Prins et al., 2009), which results in aberrant Nox2 ROS production and implicates Nox2 ROS in altered mechanotransduction (Khairallah et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khairallah et al., 2012.

claim: Nox2 ROS is upregulated early (19 d), prior to changes in the MT network.
source: However, Nox2 ROS is upregulated early (19 d; (Whitehead et al., 2010)), prior to changes in the MT network (Belanto et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2017; Khairallah et al., 2012; Prins et al., 2009), and oxidation has been shown to be a post-translational modification of the MT network (Clark et al., 2014; Landino et al., 2004; Wilson and González-Billault, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whitehead et al., 2010 and Belanto et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2017; Khairallah et al., 2012; Prins et al., 2009.

claim: Oxidation has been shown to be a post-translational modification of the MT network.
source: However, Nox2 ROS is upregulated early (19 d; (Whitehead et al., 2010)), prior to changes in the MT network (Belanto et al., 2016; Iyer et al., 2017; Khairallah et al., 2012; Prins et al., 2009), and oxidation has been shown to be a post-translational modification of the MT network (Clark et al., 2014; Landino et al., 2004; Wilson and González-Billault, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2014; Landino et al., 2004; Wilson and González-Billault, 2015.

claim: Dystrophic muscle is characterized by increased fibrosis and muscle stiffness.
source: In addition to increased Nox2 ROS production and alterations in the MT network, dystrophic muscle is characterized by increased fibrosis and muscle stiffness (Cornu et al., 1998; Cornu et al., 2001; Virgilio et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cornu et al., 1998; Cornu et al., 2001; Virgilio et al., 2015.

claim: The de-tyrosination of α-tubulin (DT-tubulin) has been proposed as a mechanism which prevents the de-polymerization of the MT network, causing an increase in muscle stiffness and dysfunction in isolated muscle cells.
source: The de-tyrosination of α-tubulin (DT-tubulin) has been proposed as a mechanism which prevents the de-polymerization of the MT network, causing an increase in muscle stiffness and dysfunction in isolated muscle cells (Kerr et al., 2015; Robison et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2015; Robison et al., 2016.

claim: Ervasti and colleagues demonstrated increased muscle stiffness with no differences in relative DT-tubulin amounts between mdx and WT mice.
source: However, Ervasti and colleagues (Belanto et al., 2016) demonstrated increased muscle stiffness with no differences in relative DT-tubulin amounts between mdx and WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Belanto et al., 2016.

claim: MT formation is sensitive to the extracellular environment.
source: MT formation is also sensitive to the extracellular environment (Myers et al., 2011; Putnam et al., 2003; Putnam et al., 2001) and increased extracellular matrix (ECM) has been implicated in increased muscle stiffness and decreased force production (Desguerre et al., 2009; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Percival et al., 2012; Rowe et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Myers et al., 2011; Putnam et al., 2003; Putnam et al., 2001.

claim: Increased extracellular matrix (ECM) has been implicated in increased muscle stiffness and decreased force production.
source: MT formation is also sensitive to the extracellular environment (Myers et al., 2011; Putnam et al., 2003; Putnam et al., 2001) and increased extracellular matrix (ECM) has been implicated in increased muscle stiffness and decreased force production (Desguerre et al., 2009; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Percival et al., 2012; Rowe et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Desguerre et al., 2009; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Percival et al., 2012; Rowe et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2014.

claim: Transgenic mdx mice expressing either a nearly full length dystrophin (DysΔ71-78-mdx) or overexpressing utrophin (Fiona) suggest that MT density and organization is independent of the level of MT de-tyrosination.
source: Intriguingly, transgenic mdx mice expressing either a nearly full length dystrophin (DysΔ71-78-mdx) or overexpressing utrophin (Fiona) suggest that MT density and organization is independent of the level of MT de-tyrosination (Belanto et al., 2014; Belanto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Belanto et al., 2014; Belanto et al., 2016.

claim: Skeletal muscle stiffness traditionally has been evaluated using either atomic force microscopy (AFM) or the passive properties of muscle measured during stretch.
source: Skeletal muscle stiffness traditionally has been evaluated using either atomic force microscopy (AFM; [Canato et al., 2010; Kerr et al., 2015; Mathur et al., 2001; van Zwieten et al., 2014]) or the passive properties of muscle measured during stretch (Hakim and Duan, 2013; Hakim et al., 2011; Lopez et al., 2008; Rowe et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Canato et al., 2010; Kerr et al., 2015; Mathur et al., 2001; van Zwieten et al., 2014 and Hakim and Duan, 2013; Hakim et al., 2011; Lopez et al., 2008; Rowe et al., 2010.

claim: AFM evaluates single muscle fiber stiffness but does not consider cell-cell interactions or the influence of the extra cellular matrix.
source: AFM evaluates single muscle fiber stiffness but does not consider cell-cell interactions or the influence of the extra cellular matrix.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' understanding of AFM methodology.

claim: Evaluating stiffness through muscle passive properties considers the series and parallel elastic components together but does not differentiate between the contributions of longitudinal (series) or transverse (parallel) tissue stiffness within overall muscle stiffness.
source: While evaluating stiffness through muscle passive properties considers the series and parallel elastic components together it does not differentiate between the contributions of longitudinal (series) or transverse (parallel) tissue stiffness within overall muscle stiffness.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' understanding of passive stretch methodology.

claim: Optical coherence elastography (OCE) has been developed as a unique method to noninvasively evaluate tissue stiffness.
source: Optical coherence elastography (OCE) recently has been developed as a unique method to noninvasively evaluate tissue stiffness (Larin and Sampson, 2017; Wang and Larin, 2014; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larin and Sampson, 2017; Wang and Larin, 2014; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Previous data indicate mdx muscle is compromised in the transverse direction.
source: Previous data indicate mdx muscle is compromised in the transverse direction (Kumar et al., 2004; Ramaswamy et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2004; Ramaswamy et al., 2011.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS production prevents the increase in α-tubulin in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: Our data confirm that α-, β-, and DT-tubulin are elevated with muscular dystrophy and extend these findings to show that eliminating Nox2 ROS production in mdx mice prevents the increase in all three forms of tubulin (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS production prevents the increase in β-tubulin in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: Our data confirm that α-, β-, and DT-tubulin are elevated with muscular dystrophy and extend these findings to show that eliminating Nox2 ROS production in mdx mice prevents the increase in all three forms of tubulin (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS production prevents the increase in DT-tubulin in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: Our data confirm that α-, β-, and DT-tubulin are elevated with muscular dystrophy and extend these findings to show that eliminating Nox2 ROS production in mdx mice prevents the increase in all three forms of tubulin (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: There is no difference in the DT-/α-tubulin ratio between WT, mdx, and p47-/-/mdx groups.
source: We found that there is no difference in the DT-/α-tubulin ratio between groups (Figure 1E), suggesting that the increase in DT-tubulin is likely due to increased α-tubulin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The increase in DT-tubulin is likely due to increased α-tubulin.
source: We found that there is no difference in the DT-/α-tubulin ratio between groups (Figure 1E), suggesting that the increase in DT-tubulin is likely due to increased α-tubulin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the DT-/α-tubulin ratio is unchanged despite increases in both DT-tubulin and α-tubulin.

claim: Khairallah et al. demonstrated Nox2 ROS production is increased in response to a polymerized MT network.
source: Khairallah et al. (2012) demonstrated Nox2 ROS production is increased in response to a polymerized MT network.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khairallah et al., 2012.

claim: Nox2 ROS production leads to increased MT disorganization in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: We found that Nox2 ROS production leads to increased MT disorganization (Figure 1G–H) and density (Figure 1I) in dystrophic diaphragm muscle which was prevented by eliminating Nox2 ROS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Nox2 ROS production leads to increased MT density in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: We found that Nox2 ROS production leads to increased MT disorganization (Figure 1G–H) and density (Figure 1I) in dystrophic diaphragm muscle which was prevented by eliminating Nox2 ROS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS prevents increased MT disorganization in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: We found that Nox2 ROS production leads to increased MT disorganization (Figure 1G–H) and density (Figure 1I) in dystrophic diaphragm muscle which was prevented by eliminating Nox2 ROS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS prevents increased MT density in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: We found that Nox2 ROS production leads to increased MT disorganization (Figure 1G–H) and density (Figure 1I) in dystrophic diaphragm muscle which was prevented by eliminating Nox2 ROS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Nox2-generated ROS increases tubulin content, MT disorganization and MT polymerization in dystrophic diaphragm muscle.
source: These results indicate that Nox2-generated ROS increases tubulin content, MT disorganization and MT polymerization in dystrophic diaphragm muscle and questions the role of DT-tubulin in MT stabilization or density.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that eliminating Nox2 ROS prevents these alterations.

claim: Increased fibrosis is a pathological hallmark of muscular dystrophy.
source: Increased fibrosis is a pathological hallmark of muscular dystrophy.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about muscular dystrophy.

claim: Diaphragm fibrosis is increased in mdx compared with WT mice.
source: In accordance with previous studies, we observed increased diaphragm fibrosis in mdx compared with WT mice (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced collagen as measured by Trichrome staining.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced collagen as measured by Trichrome staining (Figure 2A), hydroxyproline concentration(Figure 2B), and collagen I content (Figure 2C) as well as fibronectin content (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced hydroxyproline concentration.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced collagen as measured by Trichrome staining (Figure 2A), hydroxyproline concentration(Figure 2B), and collagen I content (Figure 2C) as well as fibronectin content (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced collagen I content.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced collagen as measured by Trichrome staining (Figure 2A), hydroxyproline concentration(Figure 2B), and collagen I content (Figure 2C) as well as fibronectin content (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced fibronectin content.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in dystrophic muscle resulted in reduced collagen as measured by Trichrome staining (Figure 2A), hydroxyproline concentration(Figure 2B), and collagen I content (Figure 2C) as well as fibronectin content (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Decreasing Nox2 ROS results in a significant decrease in fibrosis in the mdx diaphragm.
source: These data suggest that decreasing Nox2 ROS results in a significant decrease in fibrosis in the mdx diaphragm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing reduced fibrosis markers when Nox2 ROS is eliminated.

claim: Microtubules have been shown to be sensitive to the extracellular environment.
source: Microtubules have been shown to be sensitive to the extracellular environment (Myers et al., 2011; Putnam et al., 2003; Putnam et al., 2001) and cell-to-cell (transverse) interactions are critical in skeletal muscle force transduction (Passerieux et al., 2007; Purslow and Trotter, 1994; Ramaswamy et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Myers et al., 2011; Putnam et al., 2003; Putnam et al., 2001.

claim: Cell-to-cell (transverse) interactions are critical in skeletal muscle force transduction.
source: Microtubules have been shown to be sensitive to the extracellular environment (Myers et al., 2011; Putnam et al., 2003; Putnam et al., 2001) and cell-to-cell (transverse) interactions are critical in skeletal muscle force transduction (Passerieux et al., 2007; Purslow and Trotter, 1994; Ramaswamy et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Passerieux et al., 2007; Purslow and Trotter, 1994; Ramaswamy et al., 2011.

claim: Passive stiffness while lengthening the diaphragm to 120% Lo was increased in mdx compared with WT mice.
source: Passive stiffness while lengthening the diaphragm to 120% Lo was increased in mdx compared with WT mice, and eliminating Nox2 ROS resulted in reduced tissue stiffness compared with mdx diaphragm (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS resulted in reduced tissue stiffness compared with mdx diaphragm.
source: Passive stiffness while lengthening the diaphragm to 120% Lo was increased in mdx compared with WT mice, and eliminating Nox2 ROS resulted in reduced tissue stiffness compared with mdx diaphragm (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Transverse stiffness was increased in diaphragm of mdx mice compared with WT mice.
source: Transverse and longitudinal stiffness, using OCE, was increased in diaphragm of mdx mice compared with WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Longitudinal stiffness was increased in diaphragm of mdx mice compared with WT mice.
source: Transverse and longitudinal stiffness, using OCE, was increased in diaphragm of mdx mice compared with WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS production reduced only longitudinal stiffness in Ncf1-/-::mdx mice to WT levels.
source: Interestingly, eliminating Nox2 ROS production reduced only longitudinal stiffness in Ncf1-/-::mdx (designated as p47(-/-)/mdx) mice to WT levels (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Muscle function for all genotypes was not altered following OCE measurements.
source: Muscle function for all genotypes was not altered following OCE measurements (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Stretch induced ROS was elevated in mdx diaphragm compared with both WT and p47(-/-)/mdx diaphragm tissue.
source: We also found that stretch induced ROS was elevated in mdx diaphragm compared with both WT and p47(-/-)/mdx diaphragm tissue (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Elevated Nox2 ROS increases diaphragm stiffness in dystrophic muscle.
source: These data suggest that elevated Nox2 ROS increases diaphragm stiffness in dystrophic muscle and demonstrate Nox2 as the source of stretch induced ROS at the tissue level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that eliminating Nox2 ROS reduces stiffness.

claim: Nox2 is the source of stretch induced ROS at the tissue level.
source: These data suggest that elevated Nox2 ROS increases diaphragm stiffness in dystrophic muscle and demonstrate Nox2 as the source of stretch induced ROS at the tissue level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that eliminating Nox2 eliminates stretch-induced ROS.

claim: Stiffness measured using OCE can detect changes in tissue elastic properties based on fiber orientation.
source: In addition, stiffness measured using OCE can detect changes in tissue elastic properties based on fiber orientation and indicate a direction-dependent response to alterations in tissue stiffness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing different stiffness values in transverse vs. longitudinal directions.

claim: Increased DT-tubulin has been suggested to stabilize the microtubule network resulting in less dynamic microtubules thereby increasing tissue stiffness.
source: Increased DT-tubulin has been suggested to stabilize the microtubule network resulting in less dynamic microtubules thereby increasing tissue stiffness (Kerr et al., 2015; Robison et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2015; Robison et al., 2016.

claim: While both α- and DT-tubulin are upregulated in dystrophic muscle the ratio of DT- to α-tubulin revealed no significant difference between groups.
source: Our results demonstrate that while both α- and DT-tubulin are upregulated in dystrophic muscle the ratio of DT- to α-tubulin revealed no significant difference between groups (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fibrosis, DT-tubulin and α-tubulin significantly correlate to transverse diaphragm stiffness.
source: A linear regression analysis demonstrated that fibrosis, DT-tubulin and α-tubulin significantly correlate to transverse and longitudinal diaphragm stiffness while the DT-/α-tubulin ratio only demonstrated a significant correlation with longitudinal stiffness (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Fibrosis, DT-tubulin and α-tubulin significantly correlate to longitudinal diaphragm stiffness.
source: A linear regression analysis demonstrated that fibrosis, DT-tubulin and α-tubulin significantly correlate to transverse and longitudinal diaphragm stiffness while the DT-/α-tubulin ratio only demonstrated a significant correlation with longitudinal stiffness (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The DT-/α-tubulin ratio only demonstrated a significant correlation with longitudinal stiffness.
source: A linear regression analysis demonstrated that fibrosis, DT-tubulin and α-tubulin significantly correlate to transverse and longitudinal diaphragm stiffness while the DT-/α-tubulin ratio only demonstrated a significant correlation with longitudinal stiffness (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: A multiple linear regression analysis with either DT- or DT-/α-tubulin ratio and fibrosis revealed that the variance was no different than fibrosis alone.
source: A multiple linear regression analysis with either DT- or DT-/α-tubulin ratio and fibrosis revealed that the variance was no different than fibrosis alone (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Fibrosis accounted for 45% of the variance in the longitudinal stiffness.
source: Fibrosis accounted for 45% of the variance in the longitudinal and nearly 70% in the transverse direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Fibrosis accounted for nearly 70% of the variance in the transverse stiffness.
source: Fibrosis accounted for 45% of the variance in the longitudinal and nearly 70% in the transverse direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: While tubulin content correlates with muscle stiffness, fibrosis accounts for the majority of the variance in muscle stiffness at the tissue level.
source: These data indicate that while tubulin content correlates with muscle stiffness, fibrosis accounts for the majority of the variance in muscle stiffness at the tissue level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical analyses showing that fibrosis explains more variance than tubulin measures.

claim: Diaphragm muscle and respiratory function are compromised in mdx mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2011; Ishizaki et al., 2008; Pal et al., 2014; Percival et al., 2012.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS production protected against diaphragm alterations in young (4–6 wks) mdx mice.
source: We previously have shown that eliminating Nox2 ROS production protected against diaphragm alterations in young (4–6 wks) mdx mice (Pal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pal et al., 2014.

claim: Diaphragm function is impaired in adult (16–24 wks) mdx muscle.
source: Here, we show that diaphragm function is impaired in adult (16–24 wks) mdx muscle and eliminating Nox2 ROS partially protected against the force deficits (Figure 4A).

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS partially protected against the force deficits in adult mdx muscle.
source: Here, we show that diaphragm function is impaired in adult (16–24 wks) mdx muscle and eliminating Nox2 ROS partially protected against the force deficits (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in adult dystrophic muscle protected against alterations in diaphragm fiber cross sectional area.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in adult dystrophic muscle also protected against alterations in diaphragm fiber cross sectional area, fiber type and central nuclei Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in adult dystrophic muscle protected against alterations in fiber type.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in adult dystrophic muscle also protected against alterations in diaphragm fiber cross sectional area, fiber type and central nuclei Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in adult dystrophic muscle protected against alterations in central nuclei.
source: Eliminating Nox2 ROS in adult dystrophic muscle also protected against alterations in diaphragm fiber cross sectional area, fiber type and central nuclei Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of Nox2 ROS provides protection against pathophysiological alterations observed in dystrophic diaphragm muscle at different stages of disease pathology.

claim: Eliminating Nox2 ROS protected against decrements in respiratory rate (f) in adult mdx mice.

claim: Both transverse and longitudinal diaphragm stiffness significantly correlated with peak diaphragm force.

claim: When either transverse or longitudinal diaphragm stiffness was included with fibrosis in a multiple linear regression analysis, the variance was no different than fibrosis alone.

claim: Diaphragm MT alterations are increased in adult dystrophic muscle.

claim: Fiber type and regeneration are altered in dystrophic muscle.
